content: Programs that provide partner services, including those utilizing social network-based approaches, must actively ensure the confidentiality of client and partner data, as well as personal and medical information. Policies, regulations, standard operating procedures, and technical measures must be implemented at all levels of the health information system to safeguard patient confidentiality. Reliable strategic information depends on high-quality data systems and processes. However, data systems are often subject to limitations such as missing values, biases, measurement errors, and human errors during data entry and computation. It is essential to assess data quality to understand these limitations and confidently interpret strategic information related to HIV testing services (HTS). Routine data quality reviews can identify errors in near real-time, allowing for immediate corrections. Independent assessments of core indicators can highlight gaps and errors in reporting, while periodic in-depth reviews can focus on specific program areas. Program data are critical for monitoring quality, ensuring quality assurance, and driving quality improvement processes. Quality improvement is a continuous process aimed at enhancing performance, typically applied by health facility teams within a national quality improvement program. This involves testing changes in program services, measuring their effects over time, and using data to address gaps and improve clinical performance and health outcomes. Surveys provide valuable insights into access to HTS, attitudes toward testing, and behaviors. They are particularly useful for gathering information on testing among key populations that may be difficult to reach through programmatic data. Surveys can be conducted in health facilities, such as sexual health clinics, or in community settings to reach underserved and vulnerable populations. Questions about HIV testing behaviors, such as frequency and mode of testing, alongside other behavioral information (e.g., sexual behavior, drug, and alcohol use), can help understand HIV testing patterns. Surveys also offer opportunities to assess the acceptability of new technologies, such as self-testing. Population-based surveys, when representative and appropriately powered, can estimate the number of people who have ever tested for HIV, tested positive, and where they tested. These surveys can approximate testing and retesting frequency and help determine the proportion of people with HIV who know their status (the first “90”) and testing coverage among hard-to-reach populations. Biobehavioral surveys, which involve collecting biological samples for HIV testing, provide independent evidence of HIV prevalence and the extent to which testing programs are reaching priority groups and the general population. Comparing self-reported HIV status with biological testing results can measure the proportion of people living with HIV who have been diagnosed. Where appropriate, incidence tests can offer insights into new infections and the proportion of individuals unaware of their HIV status. Programs delivering partner services must ensure the confidentiality of client and partner data, as well as personal and medical information. However, survey findings may have limited generalizability depending on sample size and sampling strategy and should be interpreted cautiously. Surveys are resource-intensive and may take several years to yield results, which is why they are often conducted periodically (e.g., every 3–5 years) and may focus on a single key population in each cycle. Disaggregating routinely collected HTS data provides evidence for refining HTS operations. Valuable disaggregation includes breaking down data by service delivery approaches, testing modalities, priority groups, and key populations. Prioritized disaggregation should include: Age: Suggested five-year age bands (e.g., 0–4, 5–9, 10–14, 15–19, etc.). At a minimum, age should be categorized into those aged 15 years or younger and those older than 15 years. Age distribution can influence positivity rates, such as when testing is scaled up among children with a low risk of HIV infection. Sex: To detect differences in access to treatment and infection rates between men and women. Key populations: Including men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, individuals in prisons or other closed settings, sex workers, and transgender individuals. Other priority groups: Such as women attending antenatal care, patients with sexually transmitted infections, individuals attending tuberculosis (TB) clinics, those with TB symptoms, and women attending family planning services in high HIV burden settings. Geographical location: By relevant subnational administrative categorizations. HIV testing provider/venue/modality: Facilityor community-based testing, self-testing, partner services, provider-assisted referral, or social network-based HTS. Retesting: To account for individuals regularly accessing HTS, particularly those retesting due to ongoing HIV risk. To set ambitious yet attainable HTS targets, program managers need to quantify HIV prevalence while excluding those on antiretroviral therapy (ART) from both the numerator and denominator—a concept known as “treatment-adjusted prevalence.” This assumes that HTS focuses on individuals with unknown or previously negative HIV status rather than those already on ART. Over time, this indicator measures progress in reaching people with HIV who are unaware of their status and not on ART. Reviewing treatment-adjusted prevalence provides valuable insights for program managers to understand positivity rates in HTS, especially in contexts of high ART coverage. This highlights the need to focus on untested segments among those who are HIV-positive. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a selected group of indicators and disaggregation for monitoring HTS programs. These indicators align with those included in the Global AIDS Monitoring (GAM) process and WHO strategic information guidelines for HIV in the health sector. Recently updated consolidated strategic information guidelines provide detailed indicator descriptions. Indicators offer critical information at various levels: Service delivery level: Clinicians and funders require information for daily patient management and long-term planning and funding of relevant services. National and subnational levels: Health program managers need reliable and timely information to identify needs and respond effectively. Strategic information helps assess whether programs are on track in terms of access, coverage, quality, and equity and guides corrective actions where needed. Global and national levels: Ministries of health and intergovernmental agencies report progress toward specific targets. Funders use strategic information to make evidence-based decisions about resource allocation and addressing gaps. Managers and decision-makers use data to plan and coordinate health interventions from national, regional, or global perspectives.
